messages.subject: logit function in AHM1
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

for those using the R/BUGS code of our AHM1 book, please note that we are using the logit function:

logit <- function(x) log(x/(1-x))

This is not part of the base distribution of R and we did not realize this when we wrote and published the code for AHM1. So some of the AHM1 functions will break, for instance, simComm in chapter 11. A colleague is generously working at putting the AHM functions into a bona fide R package and has replaced our logit with R's qlogis, so in the future, all should run fine for everybody (and there will be help pages etc.). However, in the meantime, as a workaround you can simply execute the above definition of the logit in R before calling functions from AHM1 and then all should be fine (or I think just writing logit <- qlogis should also work).

Sorry for any inconvenience.

Best regards  -- Marc

( PS: R should really have the logit function in the base distribution ! )

messages.subject_clean: Bayesian point-transect HDS with groupsize and data-augmentation
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I am working on a point-transect bayesian HDS model for data with group size, and running into some issues adapting the model that is provided in the AHM book (chapter 9).

Due to the nature of my real-life dataset, I need to make two main modifications to the model presented in the book (section 9.2.2):

1. Point transect data (the model in the book is for line-transect data).

2. I have two abundance covariates, one continuous ("elevation") and one factor ("habitat").

I tweaked function ‘simHDSg’, which already has a point-transect option, to generate a simulated dataset with these covariates. For the factor variable, I am simulating n=3 levels using (n-1) dummy variables (my real dataset has more levels but I wanted to keep the simulation simpler to begin with).

For the analysis, I modified the BUGS model code (section 9.2.2.) for binned point-transect data using data augmentation.

I ran the model using JAGS (jagsUI package). The model seems to converge adequately. The parameter estimates for abundance covariates (habitat factor levels and elevation, beta0-beta3) are close to the data-generating values, and the estimated number of groups and of individuals are also fairly close to the data simulated.

However, estimates are rather far from data-generating values for the group size covariate intercept (alpha0) and slope (alpha1) on log(sigma) of the half-normal. Curiously, it looks like they are switched, i.e. the estimate for alpha0 is close to the true value for alpha1 and vice-vers. I suspect there may be some error(s) in my implementation o the point-transect with DA framework, but I can’t seem to find it.

I would be grateful if someone could take a look at the code and see if they can spot any errors or give me any suggestions.

Cheers,

Francisco

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I was wondering how one could incorporate information about detection probability (p) into a binary-response-type of model ? For a Poisson model of counts, when I have an estimate of p (p_hat) from somewhere, I can “up-scale” the counts by using log(p_hat) as an offset. However, the same does not seem to work for a binary response.

The context for this question is the new European Breeding Bird Atlas (http://www.ebba2.info/), where in some countries there are replicate surveys which allow estimation of p, while in others there are no replicate surveys. We were wondering whether one could use the data from the former countries to obtain an estimate of p that is specific for a protocol (i.e., point-transects versus line-transects) and for a given survey duration (for both protocols) and survey distance (only lines) or else survey area (for both). Then, assuming that survey conditions are the same in the countries with only a single replicate, one could predict p for them and use that as a correction factor in the ensuing modeling analyses, which would be based on some wiggly-covariate methods (e.g., boosted regression trees or random forests).

Any insight would be much appreciated.

Best regards  --- Marc

Marc,

The likelihood function for the logistic regression with cloglog link is equivalent to a censored Poisson model and I have showcased this as example in our 2013 MEE paper <http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12106>'s supporting info <https://github.com/psolymos/QPAD/blob/master/inst/doc/v2/QPAD_SupportingInfo.pdf> (see p. 16).This preserves the log-additivity, and works pretty well if 1's do not dominate the data -- which is rarely the case in my experience.

Not sure if other approaches, like BRT's allow to change the link function for Binomial model.

HTH,

Peter

I am working on a problem for which I am trying to identify some non-linearity in the relationship between occupancy and a covariate.

So, my question is whether anyone has done this, i.e., a hierarchical occupancy model using a GAM?

I am just starting to look around, so apologies if there is an obvious solution that I haven’t found yet. Also, I wanted to crowdsource first, mostly to stimulate discussion.

Chris

Dear Chris,

we have an example of an occupancy model with splines of a covariate in both psi and p in the AHM1 book. End of chapter 10 or so.

messages.subject: Marsh Seedeater occurrence study
messages.body_plain:
Dear hmecology users, my name is Joaquin Aldabe from Uruguay. I'm conducting a study which aim is to identify factors that affect occupancy of a globally endangered tall grassland species called Marsh Seedeater Sporophila palustris (endemic to Southern Cone of South America).

Sites were considered as 0.5 ha grassland patches along routes, and separated each other for at least 500 m (so sites are not independent; it's a unique patchy seedeater population). I already have one season dataset with 24 presence sites and about 70 absence sites. However, I did not consider imperfect detection and I suspect that false negatives may be important. So, I'm planning going back to the field this season (starting these days) and repeat each site survey, do two visits to each site (temporal replicates) and through dynamic occupancy model estimate probability of occurrence for each season as a function of covariates, considering probability of detection calculated based on this season survey and assuming there are no significant changes in observation conditions and population size. Thus, I will be able to estimate colonisation and extinction rates and assess what covariates govern them.

This approach was built with the aid of Marc Kery, who suggested me to consult it to a wider audience. So, I would really appreciate your comments.

All the best,
Joaquin

Then use those "blocks" as your "sites" (independent) and the smaller grassland patches as your repeat surveys (not independent). The Hines model will give you occupancy at the "site" level and also conditional occupancy probability at the "local" level (i.e., probability of the smaller patch within the block being occupied, given that the larger block is occupied). You can include covariates for both levels of occupancy, which is nice if you think those relationships might change at different spatial scales.
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear Joaquin,

Very interesting study!

I was just wondering about your replicates to estimate detection probability. I don't know this species, but maybe you might need to survey the temporal replicates very close in time to assure that you will estimate only detection probability. Otherwise this would be confounded with temporal emigration.
I work with dolphins, and as they present high mobility, we used a boat with observers in the bow and stern, so the duplicates are almost instantaneous. Maybe you can work with two teams (observers) at the same time (if this does not change birds behaviour and the observers are independent...). Just a thought!

All best,
Heloise

messages.body_plain:
Hey everyone!

Given the great information I was given during my last post to this group, I thought I would provide a brief update and an additional question. To analyze my aforementioned transect data, I've ultimately decided to employ unmarked's "gdistsamp()". I chose to use gdistsamp() rather than distsamp() because it seems more flexible in that it allows use of the Negative Binomial Distribution, should there be overdispersion present. I've been playing around with some of the gdistsamp() models and everything seems to be very straightforward with respect to lambda (abundance, density). I've managed to create models for lambda and predict density across habitat covariates and that sort of thing -- totally awesome.

One question I'm struggling with is related to detection probability. For example, I inserted a covariate for "observer" to evaluate whether different observers have higher detection probability for the critter than others. AIC scores suggested "yes". Model shown below:

p.observer<-gdistsamp(~1,~1,~observer, data=umf, output="density", mixture="P")

My questions are these:

1) is it legitimate to use detection covariates in this way? If struck me as a bit odd that gdistsamp() has an argument for SiteCovs but not for ObsCovs -- so I forced "observer" into the StieCovs and modeled it that way

2) my second question is concerning predictions. Assuming the method is legitimate (Question 1), in what units are the predictions made? When I use predict() on this model, my estimates for observer A=239 and B=158. I'm used to detection probability being from 0.0 to 1.0 (for occupancy, N-mixture). I assume there is a straightforward answer to this and, if so, could someone direct me to an information source so I could understand this detection concept within the HDS framework?

In spite of the challenges I've bumped into along the way here, I'm finding gdistsamp to be a very useful and exciting tool. Nice to have this in my arsenal moving forward.

Thanks a ton in advance for reading and for your previous support.
Cheers, D.J.

  alpha5[i] ~ dnorm(mu.alpha5, tau.alpha5)        # Intercept random effects

}
mu.BOD ~ dnorm(0, 0.0001)

sd.BOD ~ dunif(0, 100)
}

Hi Cody,

Both options, either including the age classes as states or modeling age with a time varying individual covariate, are valid. However, including age as further states might be more complicated due to the intial values (as you realised) and is likely to be computationally more intense compared to the other approach. Therefore I would recommend at first place using the time varying individual covariate. Regarding intital values for multistate models: it has to be kept in mind that inits for the latent states has to be given, which may or may not correspond with the observed states. Furthermore, the inits must neither contradict the model nor the observations. It can be a pain to find good ones, but with these rules it should generally work.

Kind regards

Michael

The easiest way may be to apply a linear model on the recapture probability. You can create a vector X in such a way that the occasion without capture effort gets the same number (e.g. 40). Thus:

X = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 40, 40, 40, 6, 7, ...]

The model for p then gets something like:

P[t] <- beta[X[t]]

Priors:

Beta[40] <- 0

Beta[1...39] ~ dunif(0, 1)

Best wishes

Michael

messages.subject: Burn or adapt?
messages.body_plain:
If you are using jagsUI::jags, you should probably be using the n.adapt argument more, as the default value (100) is too small for all but the simplest models.

During adaptation, the sampler parameters, eg, step size for a random-walk sampler, are tuned to give good mixing. Too little tuning does not affect the validity of the MCMC chain, but does give poor mixing, with high autocorrelation and low effective sample size.

In WinBUGS and OpenBUGS, the first part of the burn-in phase was used for adaptation, and tuning was turned off when internal criteria were met. The point of burn-in is to move away from the arbitrary starting values, and that also happens during adaptation. The only time we noticed adaptation was when burn-in was insufficient for adaptation to complete, and we could not set monitors.

JAGS has a separate adaptation phase, which is skipped if samplers do not need tuning, and the user decides how many iterations to use for adaptation.

With R2jags::jags, the entire burn-in phase is passed to JAGS as an adaptation phase. That makes sense if adaptation is necessary, but if JAGS skips adaptation we get no burn-in!

jagsUI::jags has separate arguments for n.adapt and n.burnin, but I suspect most users are like me and plug in thousands of iterations for n.burnin and leave the default for n.adapt = 100. We would get much better mixing if we used thousands of iterations for n.adapt and none for post-adaptation burn-in. But we'd have to check the trace plots (as we always do...) to pick up the cases where adaptation was skipped and burn-in is needed.

There's more on this issue at my web site here <http://mikemeredith.net/blog/2016/Adapt_or_burn.htm>.
